evidence_text: The Sharpe ratio seeks to characterize how well the return of an asset compensates the investor for the risk taken. When comparing two assets, the one with a higher Sharpe ratio appears to provide better return for the same risk
logical_form: if the Sharpe ratio characterizes risk-adjusted return, then a higher Sharpe ratio implies better risk-adjusted return

evidence_text: Ponzi schemes will have a high empirical Sharpe ratio until they fail. The empirical standard deviation before failure gives no real indication of the size of the risk being run.
mechanism: Ponzi schemes artificially inflate returns in the short term, leading to a high Sharpe ratio that masks the underlying risk.

evidence_text: A fund that sells low-strike put options will have a high empirical Sharpe ratio until one of those puts is exercised, creating a large loss. The empirical standard deviation before failure gives no real indication of the size of the risk being run.
mechanism: Selling low-strike put options generates consistent small gains, leading to a high Sharpe ratio, but the potential for a large loss is not reflected in the standard deviation.

evidence_text: Ponzi schemes will have a high empirical Sharpe ratio until they fail. A reliable empirical estimate of Sharpe ratio still requires the collection of return data over sufficient period for all aspects of the strategy returns to be observed.
mechanism: The short-term high Sharpe ratio of a Ponzi scheme can mislead investors and prevent them from collecting sufficient data to observe the true risk.

evidence_text: A fund that sells low-strike put options will have a high empirical Sharpe ratio until one of those puts is exercised, creating a large loss. A reliable empirical estimate of Sharpe ratio still requires the collection of return data over sufficient period for all aspects of the strategy returns to be observed.
mechanism: The consistently positive returns from selling puts can create a false sense of security, reducing the incentive to collect data over a long enough period to observe the potential for large losses.

evidence_text: Goetzmann, Ingersoll, Spiegel, and Welch (2002) determined that the best strategy to maximize a portfolio's Sharpe ratio, when both securities and options contracts on these securities are available for investment, is a portfolio of selling one out-of-the-money call and selling one out-of-the-money put. This portfolio generates an immediate positive payoff, has a large probability of generating modestly high returns, and has a small probability of generating huge losses.
logical_form: if a portfolio maximizes Sharpe ratio by selling options, then it generates positive payoff, high probability of modest returns, and small probability of huge losses

evidence_text: Goetzmann, Ingersoll, Spiegel, and Welch (2002) determined that the best strategy to maximize a portfolio's Sharpe ratio, when both securities and options contracts on these securities are available for investment, is a portfolio of selling one out-of-the-money call and selling one out-of-the-money put. Shah (2014) observed that such a portfolio is not suitable for many investors, but fund sponsors who select fund managers primarily based on the Sharpe ratio will give incentives for fund managers to adopt such a strategy.
mechanism: The desire to maximize Sharpe ratio incentivizes fund managers to adopt strategies that are not suitable for many investors.

The magnitude of the Sharpe ratio is sensitive to the time period over which the underlying returns are measured. The nominator of the ratio (returns) scales in proportion to time.
mechanism: The time period affects the Sharpe ratio because returns scale linearly with time.

evidence_text: The magnitude of the Sharpe ratio is sensitive to the time period over which the underlying returns are measured. The denominator of the ratio (standard deviation) scales in proportion to the square root of time.
mechanism: The time period affects the Sharpe ratio because standard deviation scales with the square root of time.

evidence_text: Most diversified indexes of equities, bonds, mortgages or commodities have annualized Sharpe ratios below 1. A Sharpe ratio consistently above 2.0 or 3.0 is unrealistic.
logical_form: if diversified indexes have Sharpe ratios below 1, then Sharpe ratios consistently above 2 or 3 are unrealistic

evidence_text: Bailey and López de Prado (2012) show that Sharpe ratios tend to be overstated in the case of hedge funds with short track records. Bailey and López de Prado (2012) propose a deflated Sharpe ratio that takes into account the asymmetry and fat-tails of the returns' distribution, sample length, and selection bias.
mechanism: The overstatement of Sharpe ratios for hedge funds with short track records motivates the development of a deflated Sharpe ratio.
